name: Calories and nutrition
intro: Where calorie counting is accurate and easy, and where the food database is wrong and slow.

apps.title: Cronometer: Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The most thorough free micronutrient tracker in the category: the only one that shows vitamins, minerals, and a full nutritional profile at no cost. A recent update degraded search results by pushing branded items ahead of generics, which seriously slows down daily logging.
apps.loved: Six years of loyal users stay for the micronutrient tracking alone. No other free app comes close.
apps.weak: After the latest update, search ranks branded products above basics, so finding 'banana' now takes several screens of scrolling.
apps.whoFor: People who track vitamins and minerals, not just calories

quotes.text: Finally committed to tracking my Marcos using an app rather than eye balling it and this app has made it beyond easy!! The bar code scanner is a cheat code forsure and it's relatively easy to build and create new meals if you are meal prepping.

I've used this app for ~6 years with varied consistency, different goals, diets, and hrt. It's probably the MOST comprehensive and customizable FREE fitness+nutrition tracker. What initially stood out to me was micronutrient tracking which idk any free app that does (or even paid!).
Finally committed to tracking my Marcos using an app rather than eye balling it and this app has made it beyond easy!! The bar code scanner is a cheat code forsure.

apps.title: Happy Scale
apps.verdict: An honest weight tracker with a strong smoothing and prediction algorithm that people use for years. The main pain point is that sync is unreliable, and some features (weigh-in notes) have moved behind a paywall.
apps.loved: The moving-average algorithm filters out daily noise and shows the real weight-loss trend.
apps.weak: Apple Health sync lags, and without it the app loses most of its purpose.
apps.whoFor: People who treat the scale as their primary weight-control tool

quotes.text: I absolutely love this app. I have been using it for many years now. It does exactly what I want to do. One thing I love about it: I am able to detect patterns in weight loss and weight gain. I also love the prediction algorithms. I can see a predicted weight on a date based on a predicted weight goal.
I love your app, but why did you add an outdated metric like BMI?
I've been using this app for the past couple of weeks and I'm already in love with it. It's so intuitive and I love being able to somewhat predict what my progress will be in the future.

Now you have to pay for a subscription to see anything. Mind you I've been using this for almost 2 years while losing 125 pounds. Now I can't see any of my history without paying. This is so ridiculous.

apps.title: Bowelle - The IBS tracker
apps.verdict: For someone with IBS or Crohn's disease, Bowelle genuinely helps identify triggers and produces data in a format that is easy to share with a gastroenterologist. The feature set is niche but well executed, and users stick around for years.
apps.loved: A timeline of symptoms and food in one log that is convenient to show a gastroenterologist.
apps.weak: Analytics do not find correlations automatically — you have to hunt for patterns in the data yourself.
apps.whoFor: People with IBS, Crohn's disease, and other chronic digestive disorders

apps.title: Nutrition Tracker: Foodnoms
apps.verdict: Foodnoms stands out for its native depth across the Apple ecosystem: it works on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Watch simultaneously, with no ads and careful attention to UI detail. The main limitations are a small food database and weak support for third-party fitness trackers.
apps.loved: Native Apple Health integration, water tracking, widgets, and Apple Watch support all in one app with no third-party compromises.
apps.weak: The food database is small and often fails to find basic items or returns inaccurate nutrient data.
apps.whoFor: Apple ecosystem users who want a native nutrition tracker without ads

apps.title: Calorie Counter - MyNetDiary
apps.verdict: MyNetDiary is one of the most accurate and usable nutrition trackers in the category: flexible unit entry, saved custom recipes, and solid handling of different goals (weight loss, gain) set it apart from competitors.
apps.loved: Users value the flexibility of entering portions in different units and an accurate database that helps track nutrition without constant errors.
apps.weak: The interface requires moving between several screens for basic actions like adding a recipe, which slows down daily logging.
apps.whoFor: People who care about data accuracy and flexible goal settings rather than pretty dashboards

quotes.text: This app is incredibly user-friendly! I really appreciate how I can enter the quantity of food, and it offers various suggestions for measurements.

apps.title: Yuka - Food & Cosmetic Scanner
apps.verdict: A barcode scanner for food and cosmetic ingredients that quickly shows a rating and explains problematic ingredients. The main flaw is an open database with insufficient moderation, leading to errors, while identical products can receive incomparable scores due to a shallow algorithm.
apps.loved: People say the app literally changed their shopping habits: they now read labels and choose cleaner products.
apps.weak: The scoring algorithm does not account for dosage and evaluates individual ingredients rather than the full formula, so similar products get different scores without a logical explanation.
apps.whoFor: People who want to quickly check a product's ingredient list in the store

apps.title: MacrosFirst - Macro Tracker
apps.verdict: The best tool for serious macro tracking: a generous free tier, accurate net-carb counting, and an active gym community. The last major update complicated navigation, frustrating long-time users, but the core product remains strong.
apps.loved: A broad free tier with honest macro tracking and no mandatory subscription from day one.
apps.weak: The latest update made the interface cluttered: six search points instead of one are confusing.
apps.whoFor: Gym-goers who track protein, fat, and carbs by the gram and need accurate analytics

quotes.text: I tried to add a simple item, the Chick-fil-A grilled patty and it wasn't an option. When I searched for it in the AI, it returned no results. When you are trying to count macros having the flexibility to add detailed items is crucial.

apps.title: MacroFactor - Macro Tracker
apps.verdict: The strongest adaptive calorie algorithm tied to real metabolism, a great UI, and a fair price. The downsides are real: the nutrient database is rough in places, female physiology is not accounted for, and support is slow.
apps.loved: Adaptive calorie calculation based on actual body weight rather than formula-based activity estimates.
apps.weak: The algorithm cuts calories to uncomfortable levels without explaining why, and adjusting manually is difficult.
apps.whoFor: Serious macro trackers willing to pay for a smart algorithm

quotes.text: I get it, the app is good for American users or ones who eat mostly packaged meals. But if you are living abroad and homecoming a variety of meals, it's hard to use. Wish there was a larger base of users with similar eating habits.

This app is truly designed for real life. The adaptive calorie and macro adjustments based on your metabolism just makes sense. Tracking your macros/calories alongside your daily weight makes so much more sense than tracking movement or activity.

This app is truly designed for real life. The adaptive calorie and macro adjustments based on your metabolism just makes sense. Tracking your macros/calories alongside your daily weight makes so much more sense than tracking movement or activity. All the trackers and estimates of caloric output is just noise.
Until it decreases your calories to an unrealistic count. I'm now at 1358 calories a day for 5-11 40 year old with my settings at the slowest.

Easy to track Macros and yes for the most part it absolutely helps you lose weight but as far as building muscle it really doesn't because it gives you less and less calories each time less protein, less carbs, I'm currently at 1200 calories and I'm always hungry.

apps.title: MacroFactor Workouts - Tracker
apps.verdict: A smart coach that adapts weights and reps based on progress rather than just logging workouts. The weak side: the interface is overwhelming for casual users, there is no Apple Watch app, and some sessions are lost due to sync glitches.
apps.loved: Automatic load progression and plan customization for home equipment without manual editing.
apps.weak: There is no way to automatically adjust the number of sets in custom programs.
apps.whoFor: Intermediate lifters who want structured progression without hiring a coach

apps.title: Carbon - Macro Coach & Tracker
apps.verdict: Carbon offers smart weekly macro adjustments based on real check-in data, and consistent users see convincing results. The weak points are a limited food database and an algorithm that sometimes prescribes dangerously low calories for active women.
apps.loved: The weekly check-in with automatic goal adjustment based on real progress replaces the work of a personal nutrition coach.
apps.weak: The food database is too small for a varied diet: users constantly have to create products manually or accept inaccuracies.
apps.whoFor: Athletes and mindful users who want an adaptive macro plan based on real progress

apps.title: Calorie Counter +
apps.verdict: A well-built tracker with a rich food database, especially strong for UK users and those migrating from other platforms. The main downside is occasional technical issues for some subscribers and the absence of a recipe builder.
apps.loved: The food database is more accurate and broader than competitors', especially for branded products.
apps.weak: There is no convenient way to enter custom recipes and calculate total nutrients per serving.
apps.whoFor: People who take calorie counting seriously and value an accurate database

apps.title: Calorie Counter by fatsecret
apps.verdict: A reliable free veteran with a huge food database and honest macro tracking. Search degraded after recent updates, and water tracking behind a paywall irritates long-time users.
apps.loved: A free database with millions of products and a clear food diary without unnecessary features.
apps.weak: After recent updates the food search broke: even 'Twix' does not come up.
apps.whoFor: Home cooks and long-term nutrition trackers who do not want to overpay

quotes.text: Useful easy to input and remembers previous foods and custom recipes. Definitely recommend. However I tend to use a few basic foods to simplify input for example I eat a meal with chicken in it. I found a good basic chicken that is measured by the ounce and ill estimate how many ounces of chicken
This app gives very few options for foods for a home cook. I do not eat out often. I also cook from scratch. I just quit My Fitness Pal. It appears this app will not suffice my as well.
It's VerySimple to use! I love how I can easily scan products!

apps.title: AteMate Food Journal (Ate)
apps.verdict: A photo food diary without forced calorie counting occupies its niche and keeps people coming back for years. The AI food analysis sometimes produces absurd ratings like 'low in nutrients' for legumes, and a subscription locks most features.
apps.loved: The app's gentle tone helps build mindful eating habits without the anxiety that strict calorie counting causes.
apps.weak: The AI meal rating often gets it wrong regardless of what is actually on the plate, and users cannot correct the verdict manually.
apps.whoFor: People who want to track eating through photos without calorie counting

apps.title: Eat This Much - Meal Planner
apps.verdict: The only meal planner in the category that generates a week's menu with an automatic shopping list and pantry tracking. For people tired of deciding what to cook it is genuinely useful, but recipes repeat, and the vegetarian selection is thin.
apps.loved: An automatic shopping list based on the weekly plan and pantry tracking save time when planning meals.
apps.weak: Recipes get repetitive quickly, and customizing for specific allergies is difficult.
apps.whoFor: People who want to plan meals a week ahead rather than just count calories

quotes.text: Could you please add a feature where we can create recipes by multi selecting foods already logged into our planner? I hate having logged something then when I make a recipe need to look up and enter the weight of each item AGAIN.

apps.title: Carb Manager: Keto & Macro Log
apps.verdict: Carb Manager is a specialized tracker with deep support for keto and low-carb diets: detailed macro tracking, fitness device sync, and a large recipe library genuinely help people stay on the diet.
apps.loved: Keto dieters note that detailed carb and sugar control helped lower blood sugar and achieve significant weight loss where other trackers fell short.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner is unreliable, and keto-compatibility detection sometimes misfires on mixed recipes.
apps.whoFor: People on keto or a low-carb diet who need detailed carb control

quotes.text: I like that it syncs to fitness devices and adjusts macros based on activity level. I like the extensive list of recipes. However, importing recipes from the web does not work.

Camera doesn't work properly, free is almost the same thing only difference is the recipes and there isn't much option. I didn't know I was going to pay for the year for the camera not to really work and me to still have to do my own search and scan items instead of just "easily" snap a photo".
This app was the primary reason I was able to drop over 50lbs and drop my blood sugar from 12.6 to 6.8. I would recommend this app to anyone trying to control their blood sugar and lose weight.

apps.title: SnapCalorie AI Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The best AI photo tracker in the category, with good accuracy within 100 calories when a dish is described in detail. A recent update worsened the interface and removed the barcode scanner, triggering a wave of complaints from regular users.
apps.loved: Fast dish recognition by photo with the ability to refine the contents and get a reasonable calorie estimate.
apps.weak: After the redesign there are more steps to log food, and removing the barcode scanner made working with packaged products harder.
apps.whoFor: People who want to count calories by photographing food rather than typing everything manually

apps.title: My Macros+ | Macro Tracker
apps.verdict: A mature macro tracker for people who take nutrition seriously: rich customization, a large food database, and responsive support. Recent updates broke the scanner and degraded search, and daily notes moved behind a paywall.
apps.loved: Flexibility in setting macro goals and ease of use once you have added your regular foods.
apps.weak: After an update the barcode scanner now requires taking a photo instead of auto-scanning and often fails to read codes.
apps.whoFor: People who track protein, fat, and carbs with precision and are used to detailed logging

quotes.text: I like this app. Especially once I got all my recipes and foods I eat in there, super quick!

I've used this app for 4 years now and have loved it. Recently the barcode scanner changed, and it's horrible. It used to automatically scan and now you need to take a picture and most of the time it can't detect the barcode. I don't understand how it got drastically worse.

I used to use this app regularly and had all of my meals named with my macro goals for that meal and a bunch of favorite foods. Now I come back to the app after a few months not counting and discover you've wiped ALL of that away and ruined all the effort I put into this app previously.

apps.title: Intermittent Fasting Tracker -
apps.verdict: The intermittent fasting timer works reliably and helps people stick to their schedule, especially those with ADHD and late-night snacking issues. The food tracker is weaker: you cannot edit a fast's start time, AI scanning is superficial, and ads in recent versions have become noticeably more aggressive.
apps.loved: The fasting timer with a widget and notifications genuinely maintains discipline and gives a sense of progress.
apps.weak: You cannot set a past start time for a fast, which throws off the statistics.
apps.whoFor: People practicing intermittent fasting who need a reliable timer above all

quotes.text: Don't get caught in the $20 for a year special that comes up. You can't track food unless you know exactly what's in it. You have to take a picture. There is no way to manually enter the name of a food to get a calorie estimate.

apps.title: Calorie Counter PRO MyNetDiary
apps.verdict: A mature and feature-rich tracker with deep analytics and solid Apple Health integration. Monetization is aggressive: users who paid for the premium version keep seeing subscription ads on top of what they already purchased.
apps.loved: Detailed nutrition and progress analytics with clear charts that are genuinely motivating.
apps.weak: After buying the PRO version the app keeps pushing subscription offers at every launch.
apps.whoFor: People who take nutrition science seriously and want data rather than just a diary

quotes.text: The app is easy to set up and supports GLP-1 use. The app will communicate back and forth with Apple Health. When you are on a GLP-1 it is more important to track protein than calorie intake and this app makes that simple.

apps.title: ZOE Health: AI Meal Tracker
apps.verdict: The app is valued for microbiome-based personalization and an emphasis on plant diversity rather than just calories. After a major update, loyal long-term users have been complaining en masse about gamification and the removal of text search in favor of mandatory photo logging.
apps.loved: Tracks the variety of plants in your diet and gives a personal score for each food.
apps.weak: After the redesign you can no longer pre-enter recipes as text, and gamification annoys an audience that came for the science.
apps.whoFor: Proponents of microbiome-based nutrition

apps.title: Food & Macro Tracker By Fittur
apps.verdict: One of the best macro trackers for ease of entry: a 'points' system for completing a day builds habits. The main problem is regular crashes during food search and no Apple Health integration.
apps.loved: Gamification through points for hitting macros keeps users on track longer.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner is unstable and often logs a completely different product than the one scanned.
apps.whoFor: People who want to track protein, fat, and carbs with a light game element

apps.title: Smart - Food Score Calculator
apps.verdict: The app calculates Weight Watchers points without monthly payments, and for its purpose it delivers honestly. The barcode scanner is broken for many users, and the restaurant database has not been updated in a long time.
apps.loved: Works for free without a subscription and quickly shows the points value of any product.
apps.weak: There is no way to keep a daily log: the app is only a points reference, not a tracker.
apps.whoFor: Weight Watchers followers who do not want to pay for the official app

apps.title: Keto Diet App － Carb Tracker
apps.verdict: A specialized keto tracker with a good restaurant food database, built-in recipes, and ready-made meal plans. The main weakness is inaccurate macro data for manually added foods and almost all functionality locked behind a paywall.
apps.loved: Keto beginners especially value the ready-made meal plans and automatic macro ratio calculation for their goal.
apps.weak: Macro data for basic foods (like chicken wings) diverge from reality, which throws off the daily carb count.
apps.whoFor: People just starting keto who want a ready plan without doing their own calculations

apps.title: ControlMyWeight
apps.verdict: A minimalist tracker with no forced registration and no ads, aimed at people who want facts without the noise. A broad CalorieKing database and custom recipe support make it a working tool, though the barcode scanner and Apple Health integration lag behind competitors.
apps.loved: No mandatory registration and no ads paired with an extensive food database is a rare combination.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner finds only a small fraction of products, so most entries are added manually.
apps.whoFor: People who want to simply log food without gamification or subscriptions

quotes.text: Recently diagnosed as Stage 2 Chronic Kidney Disease, Prediabetic. I already had Osteoarthritis and Eczema and focused on losing 30lbs gained since moving to a new state. This free mobile app has been a godsend. It's so helpful to actually see where my numbers are at any point.

apps.title: StrongrFastr Diet+Fitness AI
apps.verdict: One of the few trackers where a meal plan is generated automatically to match macros and budget, and the recipes genuinely appeal to families. Weak points: you cannot add your own food instead of a suggested item, and the app sometimes glitches like a web wrapper.
apps.loved: Automatic weekly menu generation accounting for budget and prep complexity.
apps.weak: You cannot swap a plan meal for your own or adjust portion size without rebuilding the entire plan.
apps.whoFor: People who want a ready nutrition program rather than just a calorie diary

apps.title: WeightWatchers Program
apps.verdict: WeightWatchers is a mature weight-management program with a precise points-based system, undermined by a series of UI redesigns: key flows now require extra taps, and recently eaten food is hard to find.
apps.loved: Users say the points system helped build a genuine habit of mindful eating rather than just counting calories.
apps.weak: Each major redesign breaks familiar flows: quickly adding frequent meals, viewing protein and fiber by meal, navigating between days.
apps.whoFor: People already familiar with the WW methodology who are willing to tolerate app instability

quotes.text: My number one pet peeve is the search function. It is beyond me why when I start to type in a food, the suggestions that come up are not foods that I have saved or logged recently. It is maddening. For example, when I type in Premier Protein, it brings up 5 flavors ahead of the flavor I use on a reg

apps.title: Fasting Tracker & Diet App
apps.verdict: An honest free fasting timer with no ads and no extra features. It does one thing, but with a critical limitation: you cannot edit the start or end time, making tracking inaccurate any time you forget.
apps.loved: Works without registration, without ads, and without a subscription: just a timer that counts fasting hours.
apps.weak: You cannot change the start or end time of a fast after the fact, which corrupts the entire history with a single mistake.
apps.whoFor: People practicing intermittent fasting who never forget to press the button

quotes.text: Love that it's just a simple app that works with no ads. Some features I'd love: history: let me see my fasting history in a list or better yet a calendar, widget: add a widget to support easily viewing/starting/stopping fasts.

apps.title: RP Diet Coach & Planner
apps.verdict: The Renaissance Periodization methodology genuinely works for athletes cutting or bulking, and long-term users confirm it. But a major redesign broke the interface: navigation became confusing, AI macro redistribution gets in the way of manual control, and support is nearly unreachable.
apps.loved: Meal timing around workouts and weekly macro adjustments provide structure that ordinary calorie counters lack.
apps.weak: After the redesign the app is hard to use with a non-standard schedule or varied diet: there is no quick calorie entry without creating a new product.
apps.whoFor: Athletes and bodybuilders following RP protocols who are willing to work through the interface

quotes.text: So excited that RP came out with an amazing app to help keep track each day. I found it very user friendly and love that I can duplicate meals since I eat the same thing most days. The reminders "time to eat" is so helpful since I live such a busy lifestyle...it helps me space out my food appropriately.

The app can be a great tool if you're eating chicken and rice everyday because you can measure those out one at a time. Where it struggled for me is if you're trying to make a meal prep recipe for the week. There's nowhere to create a recipe, add in how many servings or the total weight, and then add it to a day.

Downloaded RP Diet Coach in 2020 expecting macro math. Instead I got structure, sanity, and abs that showed up. This thing tells me exactly what to eat, when to eat it No food shaming. No "good vs bad" nonsense. Just "hey, eat this amount, trust the process, go live your life."

apps.title: Amino: AI Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: A free tracker with AI plate recognition and detailed nutrient breakdown that competes honestly with paid alternatives. The app loses data after crashes, and AI sometimes hallucinates nutrients even when scanning a clear label.
apps.loved: Nutrient balance analysis and specific recommendations for improving your diet directly in the meal card.
apps.weak: Manually editing after an AI error does not recalculate the overall health score.
apps.whoFor: Mindful eating beginners who care about diet quality feedback rather than just numbers

apps.title: SNAQ - Diabetes Food Tracker
apps.verdict: For a diabetic using a Libre or Dexcom, SNAQ genuinely helps lower A1c by connecting glucose and food data on one screen. After each major update something breaks, and users have to relearn the app.
apps.loved: A detailed three-hour report on glucose response to a specific meal.
apps.weak: The food database is small, and user-created recipes with custom ingredients do not calculate net carbs.
apps.whoFor: Diabetics with a Libre or Dexcom continuous glucose monitor

apps.title: mySymptoms Food Diary
apps.verdict: The only dedicated food intolerance diary in the selection rather than a calorie tracker: it helps find correlations between food and symptoms. The analysis algorithm is weak and can flag 'water' as the main trigger, and the registration flow with a nickname selection often freezes.
apps.loved: Helps identify real food triggers in chronic illness through a symptom diary.
apps.weak: The correlation algorithm gives false positives and does not always deliver useful insights after weeks of logging.
apps.whoFor: People with IBS, food allergies, or intolerances who need a symptom log

apps.title: VeSync
apps.verdict: An app for controlling Levoit smart devices (scales, air purifiers, humidifiers) with no direct relevance to nutrition or calorie tracking. The core function works reliably, but aggressive in-dashboard ads for other products irritate almost everyone.
apps.loved: Smart scale users appreciate the convenient body composition tracking over time and straightforward initial setup.
apps.weak: The app has turned into an ad platform: banners and offers to buy new devices appear right on the screen controlling your current one.
apps.whoFor: Owners of Levoit and VeSync devices for remote control

apps.title: AI Calorie Tracker by Yazio
apps.verdict: A mature tracker with a large food database and integrations, but after a series of updates it has become pushy: non-stop tips that cannot be turned off and animations slow down the basic action of adding food. Some previously free features moved behind a paywall without notice.
apps.loved: The food database is extensive and handles food from many different countries well.
apps.weak: After every meal entry, tips and animations pop up that cannot be dismissed even in the paid version.
apps.whoFor: People who eat a varied diet and can tolerate an intrusive UX in exchange for a broad food database

quotes.text: Офигенное приложение. Со 111 кг сбросил уже до 90 кг. И самое главное поменял свое пищевое поведение. Рекомендую.

Бош буквально на второй день при добавлении блюда КАЖДЫЙ РАЗ вы терроризируете СОВЕТАМИ от которых невозможно отказаться. После этого вы втираете мне платную подписку. Весь этот процесс отнимает МИНУТУ МОЕЙ ЖИЗНИ. Короче, удаляю.

apps.title: Fitia: Calorie Counter & Diet
apps.verdict: The best choice among Spanish-language trackers thanks to adapted food databases and a flexible meal planner. The scanner and recipe stability leave something to be desired.
apps.loved: The meal planner selects dishes based on available ingredients and nutrition goals.
apps.weak: Saved recipe macros change when reopened without any visible reason.
apps.whoFor: Users who want a ready meal plan rather than a blank diary

quotes.text: I paid for a year of premium. However, I often have to add my own barcodes for stuff or stuff from restaurants. You'd think I'd be able to search "chik fil a sauce" and find it easily but no.

apps.title: Stupid Simple Keto Diet App
apps.verdict: For keto eating the app offers more customization depth than most alternatives, and long-term users genuinely maintain their weight for years. The main weaknesses are occasional total data loss and no fiber tracking for net carbs.
apps.loved: Keto veterans value the simple setup and the fact that the app keeps them on track without unnecessary noise.
apps.weak: The app periodically wipes all history and saved favorite foods, forcing users to re-enter everything.
apps.whoFor: People following a keto diet who want a specialized tracker without clutter

apps.title: Calories and nutrition tracker
apps.verdict: A simple tracker with a large food database that works well for basic calorie and macro counting. The core problem: the database was crowd-sourced without verification, so the same product often has several entries with different and incorrect values.
apps.loved: Meal reminders and the ease of adding dishes through a large food database.
apps.weak: The user database has many duplicates and inaccurate entries, especially for fast food and scanned barcodes.
apps.whoFor: People starting to track their diet who want a simple free tool

apps.title: CalBot: AI Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: Photo food recognition works accurately enough to replace manual entry and covers local restaurants and unusual dishes. The five-entry-per-day limit on the free plan and variable macro accuracy undermine confidence in the results.
apps.loved: Describing a dish in text instead of searching a database significantly speeds up logging a familiar diet.
apps.weak: The same product entered three different ways gives three different calorie answers.
apps.whoFor: Users who eat varied food and do not want to spend time searching for every dish

apps.title: Mealo: Pocket AI Fitness Coach
apps.verdict: An appealing AI photo-tracking concept, but the GPT engine regularly gets portions and calories wrong and customer support does not respond. The foundation is still unstable.
apps.loved: You can photograph a plate and get a macro breakdown without manual entry.
apps.weak: The AI systematically hallucinates portions and assigns food to the wrong day when a photo is uploaded.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who value speed of entry over numerical accuracy

apps.title: Lose It! – Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: Lose It! is a functional calorie counter with a broad food database and macro support, but aggressive monetization through ads after every action and previously free features moving behind a paywall significantly reduce the value of the free version.
apps.loved: Long-term users say the app helps build lasting dietary control and genuinely works for weight loss with consistent use.
apps.weak: The food database contains user entries with incorrect data, and recipes are difficult to create due to a confusing interface.
apps.whoFor: People willing to buy a subscription for a clean ad-free experience

quotes.text: I want to give this app five stars, but after fighting for half an hour with the "create recipe" workflow, I got angry at the app. Any UI that shows two check marks on the same screen needs to be redesigned. Somehow I ended up with half a dozen recipes with the same name, but different ingredients.

I have two issues with this app: I can enter my weight only in pounds. I want to use kg. There should be an option to choose. I don't measure my olive oil in ml, I just want to be able to put in weight in grams.

apps.title: 8fit Workouts & Meal Planner
apps.verdict: A combo app for workouts and meal planning that stopped receiving updates roughly two years ago. Those who used it while it was functional lost 25 to 40 kg thanks to short HIIT sessions and weekly meal plans, but now login and subscription payment often do not work.
apps.loved: Users who started in 2017 to 2019 praise the 20-minute workouts — ideal for people with ADHD and packed schedules.
apps.weak: The app is effectively abandoned: Google login is broken, subscriptions cannot be purchased, and some workouts were removed without replacements.
apps.whoFor: People who want to combine short workouts with a ready meal plan — if the app launches at all

apps.title: Nutritionix Track
apps.verdict: A tracker with a good food database and an honest free model, but with a critical reliability problem: the server regularly goes offline for days or weeks, and during each outage some users lose their entire food history and custom recipes.
apps.loved: A large restaurant and prepared-food database makes tracking easier for people who frequently eat out.
apps.weak: Food history and custom recipes are periodically wiped during technical outages with no recovery option.
apps.whoFor: People willing to accept an unreliable infrastructure in exchange for free tracking with a restaurant database

quotes.text: I am done with this app. It IS great, tracks my protein and carb intake very well. But for the third time I have lost all of my previous numbers, custom foods, all my statistics. I know it's free, but if I have to KEEP entering food information every time this randomly erases all of my info, it's not worth it.

Great when it works, but twice now it has crashed or been offline for days "for major improvements" that never materialize. The worst part of this is that ALL your stored data (including the recipes you've laboriously built and saved) is erased!

apps.title: Foodvisor - AI Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: Gamification and visual style keep users logging for months, but the functional core is shaky: the scanner often misses, portion setup is unintuitive, and the color-rating algorithm for meals raises doubts.
apps.loved: Game quests and flora progress motivate keeping a food diary without willpower.
apps.weak: The barcode and photo scanner frequently returns incorrect data, and correcting it is harder than re-entering from scratch.
apps.whoFor: People who need motivation to stick with tracking rather than precision to the gram

quotes.text: I like the quests and flora are cute and it's a fun way to encourage people to use the app consistently. However, the scanning function for logging food is nearly always incorrect.

This app is super cute overall but the way it logs food is not intuitive. I don't measure things in grams or ounces and that is how it wants you to log most foods. It should have it in cups or pieces of fruit/vegetable.

apps.title: Stupid Simple Macro Tracker
apps.verdict: The simplest interface in the category: no extra screens, fast entry. But the barcode scanner is unreliable, ads in the free version have become aggressive, and recent updates brought freezes while editing.
apps.loved: A 'here is how much more you can eat' prompt right below the food entry field helps make decisions before the first bite.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner does not read most everyday products, forcing users to enter everything manually.
apps.whoFor: People who want an extremely simple free tracker with no extra features

apps.title: calorie.ai - Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: A free tracker with AI food entry and a barcode scanner valued for its simplicity and lack of a subscription. However, search and the scanner have periodically broken completely, and AI sometimes gives widely varying estimates for the same dishes.
apps.loved: A free core without a subscription and a straightforward interface without unnecessary screens.
apps.weak: The food database is small, search breaks after updates, and AI gives inconsistent results for the same dishes.
apps.whoFor: People who want to count calories for free without extra features

apps.title: Value Diary - Weight Loss Diet
apps.verdict: The only reliable alternative tracker for older Weight Watchers plans that the official app no longer supports. Problems restoring a subscription after switching phones spoil the experience for long-term users.
apps.loved: Support for WW Purple, Blue, and Green plans at a significantly lower subscription cost.
apps.weak: The food database is sparse in the free version, and the barcode scanner fires inconsistently.
apps.whoFor: Classic Weight Watchers fans whose plan was discontinued or made more expensive

apps.title: 1st Phorm
apps.verdict: The app combines a food diary, workouts, and live coaches in one place, and for dedicated brand fans it genuinely works. But stability is poor: data disappears, macros do not update without an app restart, and notifications fire twenty times in a row.
apps.loved: A live coach inside the app that competitors do not offer.
apps.weak: The app does not save custom products and resets progress on glitches.
apps.whoFor: 1st Phorm supplement buyers who want a single hub with a coach

apps.title: Macro Tracker - Keto Diet App
apps.verdict: A deliberately minimalist counter with no database and no subscription, suitable for people who know their macros by heart. The critical flaw is one: an entered record cannot be corrected, only the entire day can be reset.
apps.loved: No registration, no ads, no subscription: just sliders for protein, fat, and carbs.
apps.weak: No individual entry can be edited or deleted — only the entire day can be wiped.
apps.whoFor: Experienced keto dieters who want a bare counter with no frills

apps.title: Polar Beat: Running & Fitness
apps.verdict: A companion app for Polar heart rate monitors that works when a stable connection is established. Bluetooth connectivity is unreliable, there is no Live Activities support on the lock screen, and the sports list was unexpectedly cut in recent updates.
apps.loved: With a stable connection it delivers accurate real-time heart rate zone data better than Apple Watch.
apps.weak: No Live Activities — to see your heart rate during a workout you have to unlock the phone every time.
apps.whoFor: Owners of Polar chest heart rate monitors willing to tolerate unreliable Bluetooth

quotes.text: I've used this app for over 12 years and rated it 5 stars for all those years. The data integrated with all previous versions of my iPhones. I just upgraded to the iPhone 17 Pro. It no longer pushes calorie data over to the Apple health app.

apps.title: Diet & Food Tracker: EatWell
apps.verdict: The app draws users in with its design and the AI dish recognition feature, but that key tool is unstable and frequently returns an error. Batch-adding multiple items was removed in an update, portions are hard to configure, and some users note an unhealthy 1,000-calorie minimum.
apps.loved: When AI recognition works it genuinely removes logging friction and gives an accurate nutrient breakdown.
apps.weak: You cannot add multiple items in one action: each product must be entered individually, which slows down diary keeping.
apps.whoFor: Users who want to log food by photo and do not mind working with an unstable tool

apps.title: Calo: AI Food Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: Photo recognition draws users in, but the food database is thin, accuracy is inconsistent, and technical quality has declined: the app starts freezing after a few days of use.
apps.loved: Fast photo recognition of dishes without having to search for a product manually.
apps.weak: The same dish shows different calories across different photos, making the data unreliable.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who need a quick start without manual entry

quotes.text: I love this app because it counts calories along with protein, carbs and water. My only issue with it is I wish it had a repeat a meal on it. I pretty much eat the same thing for breakfast and I have to put it in every day. The photo calorie count is amazing.

apps.title: Calorie Counter - Calory AI
apps.verdict: The app works as a convenient calorie counter with a clean interface, but a large-scale paywall move for previously free features broke trust with a big part of the audience. For users who pay, AI voice entry and scanning provide real speed gains, though AI accuracy is low.
apps.loved: The ring visualization of the daily calorie limit and fast food search make daily diary keeping pleasant.
apps.weak: AI dish recognition and voice entry need constant manual verification due to low accuracy.
apps.whoFor: Users who already bought a lifetime pass and have been keeping a diary for years

apps.title: Calorie Counter by Pro Tracker
apps.verdict: A mature tracker with a solid food database that some users have relied on for six years and praise for stability. The core problem: developers have repeatedly moved previously free features behind a paywall without warning, which has seriously eroded trust.
apps.loved: The barcode scanner finds products from Whole Foods and Costco that other apps do not have.
apps.weak: Developers move previously accessible features behind a paywall without announcement, and data is sometimes lost after updates.
apps.whoFor: People who track macros without needing complex AI features

apps.title: Daily Tracker Journal & Diary
apps.verdict: Once a very flexible tracker with a long history, but the move to a subscription model broke data access for some users and alienated those who had paid for a lifetime license. The product value is real, but trust has been damaged.
apps.loved: Full freedom to customize fields and templates plus clear multi-year observation charts.
apps.weak: When exporting data or syncing between devices, Google authorization is regularly required and often fails.
apps.whoFor: Methodical people who want to keep several trackers in one place

apps.title: Noom Weight Loss, Food Tracker
apps.verdict: Noom combines behavioral eating education with tracking and coach access, which genuinely works for some users, but the interface has become heavy and overloaded with gamification after several updates.
apps.loved: The approach combining behavioral psychology, a food diary, and a live coach in one place helps people change their relationship with food rather than just count calories.
apps.weak: No fiber tracking at a premium subscription price, and the push notification reward animations ('seeds') that cannot be turned off irritate even loyal users.
apps.whoFor: People who need behavioral support and a coach rather than just a calorie counter

quotes.text: The psychology is good but the biggest place where Noom is failing its paid subscribers is there is no fiber tracking. In 2026 when fiber & protein are what we are being told is most important, we can't track both with a $200 subscription? When so many of us are on GLP-1s?
Excellent platform - it truly works and I've achieved results I was looking for. Now I'm in the habit of logging meals, and doesn't feel like a huge burden. Highly recommend.

Added the concept of seeds that I do not care about. But they will not let you opt out of seeds. The annoying part is every so often they give you the stupid seeds as rewards and freeze up the screen for 30 seconds.
The gamification has been taken to the extreme and it seems like I can't log a meal without 5 interruptions.

apps.title: Capy Diet: Fun Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The capybara pet gamification genuinely motivates some users, and basic food tracking works. But the rewards shop is empty, support does not reply, and some food entry mechanics are broken.
apps.loved: Gamification through pet customization makes daily tracking less boring.
apps.weak: The reward mechanic (the capybara shop) has been abandoned by developers and not updated in a long time.
apps.whoFor: Young users and teens who find a standard food diary boring

apps.title: Fooducate: Nutrition Coach
apps.verdict: A once-strong tracker with a unique letter-grade food quality rating that now suffers from an outdated database, an inability to edit added foods, and unreliable performance. Long-term users document regression rather than progress.
apps.loved: The idea of grading foods from A to D by nutritional value rather than just calories still appeals to people who want to understand food quality, not just numbers.
apps.weak: The database covers non-American and niche products poorly, and user-added items cannot be edited after saving.
apps.whoFor: People who want to assess product quality by composition rather than count calories

quotes.text: This app is good but a lot of foods need to be entered even for large chain grocery items that are generic branded. And I don't understand why it's been 20 years but there is no watch feature?

apps.title: MyFitnessPal: Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: MyFitnessPal was once the industry standard for calorie tracking. Today it is fragmented by several waves of redesigns: the food database is extensive but data accuracy is unreliable, and key features like voice entry and the scanner are unstable.
apps.loved: A large food database and fitness tracker integrations cover most typical diets without manual entry.
apps.weak: Nutrient values in the user database are regularly inaccurate, and editing or verifying them without a subscription is impossible.
apps.whoFor: People who already keep a food diary and want fitness device integration

quotes.text: I've been enjoying this app and its ease of use! It fully integrates with my training app and allows my fitness trainer to provide regular feedback!

apps.title: Nutrition Coach: Food tracker
apps.verdict: A nutrition tracker with a meal planner and Apple Health integration that lost basic features after a major redesign: gram-based entry was removed, saving meals does not work, and calories randomly double. Users who return after a year do not recognize the app.
apps.loved: Before the redesign, long-term users praised a clean minimal interface and meaningful weight-loss results over two years.
apps.weak: The update removed gram and weight-based portion entry, leaving only servings — a critical regression for people who weigh their food.
apps.whoFor: People managing their weight without deep nutrient tracking

quotes.text: I've been using this app for 3 years but the new update is not good at all. I prefer to track food by weight and volume, however the update only allows me to track food by servings.

apps.title: Healthify: AI Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: Combines nutrition tracking with access to real dietitians and an AI assistant, and for some users the coaching component works well. Core product problems: AI photo recognition gives a 100-calorie spread for the same photo, and Garmin sync does not work.
apps.loved: Live dietitian coaches who adapt the plan to a specific lifestyle.
apps.weak: The AI photo tracker is inconsistent: the same dish is calculated differently on different days.
apps.whoFor: People who want to work with a personal dietitian through an app

apps.title: Arise: AI Food Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: A clean interface and third-party integrations make a good first impression, but the food database is oriented toward the European market and does not cover common American products. The absence of previous-day browsing makes progress analysis impossible.
apps.loved: The badge and reward system maintains motivation in the first few weeks of use.
apps.weak: Portion units are limited to ounces with no gram or cup alternatives.
apps.whoFor: Users in Europe or those who want to combine calorie tracking with fitness goals

apps.title: My Diet Coach - Weight Loss
apps.verdict: Previously the app stood out with an avatar and game mechanics that motivated users — one reviewer lost 89 kg on the old version. After the redesign the interactivity disappeared, and data loss on glitches happens regularly.
apps.loved: The old version with an avatar and bright colors created real motivation and an engaging experience.
apps.weak: No backup: switching phones or deleting the app means losing all history completely.
apps.whoFor: People who need a simple food diary that works offline

quotes.text: I like this app. It's really useful. But I've now lost all my data three times whenever they decide to update something or whatever. It's really demoralizing and frustrating for something that feels so important to me.

apps.title: BetterMe: Health Coaching
apps.verdict: BetterMe positions itself as a fitness coaching app rather than a nutrition tracker: workouts and pelvic exercises are central, while the food diary is rough and inconvenient.
apps.loved: Users looking for structured progressive workouts report real gains in flexibility and strength within the first few weeks.
apps.weak: Food entry is significantly harder than in dedicated apps: there is no flexibility for meal swaps or personalization for dietary restrictions.
apps.whoFor: Fitness beginners who care more about movement than precise calorie tracking

apps.title: Lifesum: AI Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: Lifesum was a respected nutrition tracker with an attractive design, but the switch to AI-based food entry brought instability: data does not save, the calorie limit resets on its own, and AI systematically misjudges portions.
apps.loved: Experienced users note that restaurant meal estimation by photo works noticeably better than competitors once you learn the app.
apps.weak: After switching to AI entry the app regularly loses logged data and offers no way to return to manual entry as the default mode.
apps.whoFor: People who value design and can tolerate instability in exchange for convenient AI scanning

apps.title: Keto diet app－Low carb manager
apps.verdict: A basic keto tracker with a limited free tier (5 to 6 products per day) and a weak database where the barcode scanner frequently returns wrong carb values. The app deletes data on crashes and does not allow editing added products.
apps.loved: The few satisfied users value a simple interface and automatic macro adjustment when weight changes.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner regularly returns incorrect carb data, which is critical for keto where precise counting matters most.
apps.whoFor: People who want the cheapest keto tracker and can accept inaccuracies

apps.title: Diet & Meal Planner by GetFit
apps.verdict: The app offers ready-made meal plans with recipes and shopping lists, and when it loads the basic scenario works reasonably well. But it regularly stops opening for weeks at a time, and the ingredient entry interface got significantly more complex after an update.
apps.loved: Ready plans with recipes and an automatic weekly shopping list.
apps.weak: Ingredient search became inconvenient after an update, and the app periodically refuses to open for hours.
apps.whoFor: People who want a ready meal plan rather than keeping a diary themselves

apps.title: Intermittent Fasting Hero Diet
apps.verdict: An intermittent fasting timer that works simply and without fuss, valued by people who need a pure hour counter. But session storage is unreliable: fasting history disappears, making progress tracking impossible.
apps.loved: A minimal fasting timer without an overloaded interface.
apps.weak: The app loses fasting history and logs users out after a few days.
apps.whoFor: People practicing intermittent fasting who need a minimal timer

apps.title: Zero: Fasting & Food Tracker
apps.verdict: Zero is a minimalist intermittent fasting timer that worked as a simple clean tool, but after moving to a mandatory subscription it lost its core appeal: there is effectively no free access to the main feature.
apps.loved: When it was available, the visual 'fat-burning flame' and simple fast timer helped people sustain long fasting windows.
apps.weak: The app no longer works as a precise tracking tool: you cannot go back and log a missed meal, and users find the macro recommendations inaccurate.
apps.whoFor: People who practice intermittent fasting and are willing to pay just for a timer

quotes.text: The flames when peak fat burn is happening are exceptionally great motivation to KEEP GOING. I trying have been enjoying tracking my meals and water intake. Planning to purchase the subscription once my month trial runs out. Love it!
I have lost 30 pounds in the first 3 months of using this app. This has quite literally been a life changer.
The flames when peak fat burn is happening are exceptionally great motivation to KEEP GOING.

apps.title: Habit Tracker
apps.verdict: A habit tracker with a clean interface and widgets that has no relation to nutrition or calories. Key complaints: device sync breaks, lifetime purchase activations fail, and history resets when a goal is changed.
apps.loved: Bright colors, a convenient habit-marking swipe, and a lock-screen widget are liked by most users.
apps.weak: Changing a goal destroys all history, and iCloud sync reliably fails after a device change.
apps.whoFor: People who need to track up to 6 habits for free with no nutrition component

apps.title: Calorie Counter & Food Tracker
apps.verdict: The app looks simple but the food database is incomplete, calories for many items are listed inaccurately, and adding unfamiliar food is a challenge. Users who figure out the interface praise the ease of keeping a diary, but most give up within the first few days.
apps.loved: A home-screen widget and simple entry for common dishes appeal to people with a standard diet.
apps.weak: The food database is small, incorrect data cannot be fixed, and the barcode scanner frequently fails to find products.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who just need a food diary with no deep analytics

quotes.text: Good for Calories, Fat, Carbs and Protein, what would push this 5 stars for me is more macro nutrients/Micronutrients like Fiber etc.

apps.title: Food Diary See How You Eat Log
apps.short: Food Diary See How You Eat Log
apps.verdict: A photo food diary without calorie counting suits people with GI issues or those who just want to see their diet. But aggressive ads in the paid version, data loss, and an inconvenient PDF export make the experience unreliable.
apps.loved: Scrolling through a photo feed of meals from several days ago helps identify the cause of a reaction to a product.
apps.weak: Upgrade banner prompts appear on literally every tap, even for paying users.
apps.whoFor: People with food intolerance who need a visual nutrition log

apps.title: EatWise - Meal Reminder
apps.verdict: The app does exactly one thing: remind you to eat on schedule, and it manages that when it works. Several consecutive updates broke the critical notification function and caused crashes, which is unacceptable for a meal reminder.
apps.loved: A clean interface without extra noise — well suited for people with suppressed appetite from medication or eating disorders.
apps.weak: There is no 'ate' button in the watch notification, and notifications stop arriving after updates.
apps.whoFor: People who only need a meal-time reminder

apps.title: Calorie Deficit Calculator
apps.verdict: An app with an appealing concept but systemic reliability problems: the scanner stopped working, food cannot be added, and data is lost on restart. Users note regression compared to earlier versions.
apps.loved: Simple logic and a free food database with restaurants and fast food attract beginners.
apps.weak: The recipe builder does not allow setting a gram-based portion — only whole or fractional servings.
apps.whoFor: Calorie-counting beginners who value simplicity over detailed settings

apps.title: FitHub - AI Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: The app positions AI as its main value, but the scanner gives contradictory results on two consecutive attempts and user-entered data changes by itself. Account loss after an update for several users is a critical warning sign.
apps.loved: Voice food entry lowers the barrier for people who are reluctant to type each product manually.
apps.weak: AI scanning systematically gets calories and protein wrong, and correcting the data is inconvenient.
apps.whoFor: People who want to try AI tracking and can accept low initial accuracy

quotes.text: i love the idea of just scanning an item and going about my day. but it seems to be very inaccurate sometimes. it doesn't make sense to scan an item that literally says 15G of protein on the front only for the app to say it's 32G.

I actually really like this app. Being able to input foods and accurately track my macros helps me stay on track. My qualm is where is the fiber tracker? We are focusing more on overall wellness than ever before.

apps.title: BitePal: Food Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: An AI tracker that photographs food but misses by 400 to 800 calories and confuses chicken with chips. Several users lost a month of data with no recovery through support.
apps.loved: The idea of photographing a plate instead of manually searching for products is convenient for low-effort tracking.
apps.weak: Recognition accuracy is too low for real dietary control — the margin of error can reach 800 kcal per meal.
apps.whoFor: People who only need a rough sense of balance rather than precise counting

apps.title: Cal AI - Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: Cal AI bets on photo dish recognition, but calorie estimation accuracy is unreliable even when scanning a barcode, and the absence of fitness tracker integrations and scant nutrient detail make it a toy rather than a working tool.
apps.loved: Users are attracted by the instant photo recognition idea, and for familiar home-cooked food or restaurant items it sometimes works surprisingly well.
apps.weak: Calorie recognition when scanning a barcode regularly gives wrong results, and suggested macro targets users describe as simply incorrect.
apps.whoFor: People who want quick approximate food control without deep analytics

quotes.text: If you're someone who just want to see or have some fun with tracking what you eat on calories and basics then this is perfect. If you're looking for ANYTHING serious or more in depth passed calories, fats and protein intake. It doesn't do a good job with labels at getting all the facts down.
I'm pretty amazed that it can even identify japanese home cooked meals. I love this app. Fun to use too

I like using this app it takes the effort out of monitoring my exercise, and calorie intake. However, I have linked it to Apple health and it has only retrieved my weight four times in about two months! I'm sure this is an easy fix.
I just added a food using the barcode and it was still wrong! I don't understand how an app can be so wrong especially when I scanned the barcode!

apps.title: Eato®: Calorie Tracker
apps.verdict: The idea of photographing a dish instead of manual entry is appealing, and some users do achieve results. But AI regularly gets portions and calories wrong, data can change without the user knowing, and losing all history on reinstall makes the tool unreliable.
apps.loved: Photo scanning of a plate reduces logging friction and allows people who previously gave up on tracking to reach their goal.
apps.weak: Calorie values change spontaneously after saving, making the diary untrustworthy.
apps.whoFor: People just starting to count calories who can accept approximate accuracy

quotes.text: I love this app. Calorie counting is simple. Take a picture of my plate, and the app figures calories for the entire meal. No more looking up each individual food. I also love the hydration portion.

apps.title: Pro Cal - AI Calorie counter
apps.verdict: A clean interface hides serious problems: the AI scanner is unreliable for real tracking, features are removed without warning, and support goes silent. Users leave disappointed more often than satisfied.
apps.loved: A clean and fast interface; photo scanning handles simple dishes.
apps.weak: AI miscounts portions for unpackaged foods, and there is no way to set an amount in grams.
apps.whoFor: People who want an aesthetically pleasing tracker for simple dishes and do not expect precision

quotes.text: The app is pretty good, nice easy ui, accurate ai scanning, barcode scanner, and search database. The only thing that's missing is to be able to track your food using the amount of grams it is. For example searching egg whites and saying 50g of egg whites.

apps.title: Kalo - AI Calorie Tracking
apps.verdict: AI scanning works reasonably, but data accuracy is unstable: one dish gets 250 kcal instead of a real 1,050. Navigation is inconvenient, dishes cannot be deleted, and the logging date often resets.
apps.loved: Photo-based food recognition lowers the barrier for users who do not want to enter data manually.
apps.weak: Nutrients cannot be entered manually if a dish is not found in the app's database.
apps.whoFor: Users who want to photograph a plate instead of scanning barcodes

apps.title: HitMeal－Calorie & Food Tracker
apps.verdict: A tracker with an attractive interface but a broken barcode scanner that does not work for most users and chaotic cross-device sync. Some users discovered all data for six months had been reset.
apps.loved: The interface is intuitive and uncluttered — easy for beginners to navigate.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner fails to read most packaging, and manual entry takes too long.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who are fine with manually logging calories without scanning

quotes.text: The app is great, the UI is easy to understand and the layout is very beginner friendly. I love the protein, carb and fat layout but a few suggestions: we should be able to see micronutrients too at least fiber, iron and vitamins as these nutrients are also important to people that track their meals.

apps.title: Baby Tracker.
apps.verdict: A good concept and a clean design, but the app fails to save entries about half the time, and the timer fires without recording anything. New parents cannot afford an unreliable tracker.
apps.loved: Clean and clear visual design without unnecessary elements.
apps.weak: No shared mode for two parents, even though all competitors support it.
apps.whoFor: New parents tracking feeds and sleep for a baby on their own

apps.title: FastEasy: Intermittent Fasting
apps.verdict: An intermittent fasting timer with a basic food diary that charges up to 39 dollars a month for functionality available in dozens of free alternatives. Masses of reviews describe being unable to cancel the subscription and charges continuing after deletion.
apps.loved: Some users value the visual timer with fasting phases and real-time explanation of what is happening in the body.
apps.weak: Food entry does not work for most new users: the add-meal button leads only to saving, not to an entry form.
apps.whoFor: People looking for a simple fasting timer who do not plan to subscribe

quotes.text: I use FastEasy every day. I love having the immediate feedback as to where I am in time. Additionally, I like knowing the benefits I'm receiving as I proceed along the 16 hour timeline.

apps.title: AI Calorie Counter - Appediet
apps.verdict: The app broke trust with its audience: users who had relied on it for free for years found one day that product search was locked behind a subscription. Functionally the tracker was simple and handled the job until that point.
apps.loved: Barcode scanning and food photos in one place are convenient as long as they are accessible.
apps.weak: Basic product search unexpectedly moved behind a paywall, making the app useless for existing users.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended at this time due to unstable access terms

apps.title: CaloCare: AI Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The AI coach confuses meals, gives advice 'for tomorrow' about 'yesterday's food,' and recipe serving sizes are absurd (4 chicken breasts per serving). Photo recognition is unstable: green beans get added sugar.
apps.loved: Photo recognition in good lighting works quickly and makes a strong first impression.
apps.weak: The AI assistant disappears from an account without warning and support does not respond.
apps.whoFor: People looking for a Noom alternative and willing to tolerate instability for a lower price

apps.title: MyDiabetes: Sugar & Meal Log
apps.verdict: A blood sugar and meal tracker with a clean interface, but surrounded by too many reports of unexpected charges and an inability to unsubscribe. The app itself is unstable: goals change on their own.
apps.loved: Quick glucose and food entry in one place helps see patterns throughout the day.
apps.weak: Meal plan recipes are out of touch with reality: exotic ingredients that are hard to find.
apps.whoFor: Diabetics who need a simple glucose log without complex analytics

apps.title: CalDiet - Food Analysis Pal
apps.verdict: An AI tracker with photo recognition that doubles calories when scanning a barcode, calculates absurd targets (1,200 kcal for someone 183 cm tall and 113 kg), and has no functioning support. There are complaints about unauthorized charges.
apps.loved: Photo food recognition identifies the dish correctly in about 80% of cases, reducing logging effort.
apps.weak: The barcode scanner doubles the product's calorie content, making tracking dangerously inaccurate.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended — too many systemic problems with accuracy and support

quotes.text: I paid 40 dollars to have this app for the year and I like it but I am so bothered that I can't log one tablespoon of something or the specific amount I ate. To be more specific, I can only say I ate 1/4, or 1/2, or 3/4, or all of it which is not enough.

apps.title: MenuFit - Healthy Eating Out
apps.verdict: A product with a non-viable core: dish data diverges from real menus, AI recommends non-existent items, and calories are noticeably understated. Business practices are also problematic — a promised trial period charges money immediately.
apps.loved: The idea of finding the healthiest items on a restaurant menu is useful for frequent diners.
apps.weak: The menu database is outdated and the app suggests dishes the restaurant no longer serves.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended for anyone — the product is too rough

apps.title: Welmi - Calorie Counter & Diet
apps.verdict: Behind a high rating there is almost no real user experience. The few substantive reviews describe functionality as basic, and complaints about paying for any action at all repeat in several languages.
apps.loved: A neat onboarding flow with personalized nutrition goals.
apps.weak: Adding any product requires a paid subscription — there is almost no free core.
apps.whoFor: Hard to identify a real audience due to the absence of genuine reviews

apps.title: Diabetes food tracker - Gococo
apps.verdict: Designed for diabetics, but the implementation is weak: AI identifies a dish correctly only half the time, data vanishes without a trace, and getting started requires completing a lengthy questionnaire with personal questions. There is almost no real value for glucose management.
apps.loved: The idea of linking eating to blood sugar levels resonates strongly with those who got to try it.
apps.weak: Photo dish recognition fails half the time and arbitrarily inflates protein grams whenever a record is edited.
apps.whoFor: Diabetics willing to tolerate unstable performance in exchange for a specialized focus

quotes.text: Very useful determining food impact on glucose levels
Why can't calorie goals be put in for weight maintenance or even gain? Not all diabetics need to lose weight.

apps.title: ‎Calorie Counter: Food Tracker
apps.verdict: The app is positioned as a tracker but in practice is a subscription funnel with aggressive upsells. Recipe filters do not work (a 'no nuts' filter shows almond milk), and the scanner is off by a factor of three on calories.
apps.loved: Notifications and a streak counter help avoid forgetting daily logging.
apps.weak: The weekly shopping plan does not consolidate products across multiple days, making the feature useless.
apps.whoFor: People just starting to count calories who do not know better free alternatives exist

quotes.text: Good for Calories, Fat, Carbs and Protein, what would push this 5 stars for me is more macro nutrients/Micronutrients like Fiber etc.

apps.title: Lean: AI Macro Tracker
apps.verdict: The AI macro tracker concept sounds appealing, but the food database is too small and the scanner works intermittently, so almost everything must be entered manually. For a paid app this is unacceptable.
apps.loved: A simple operating principle: the app calculates how much more you can eat.
apps.weak: Fractional portions cannot be entered, and macro scaling when multiplying a serving does not work correctly.
apps.whoFor: Beginners who want to start tracking protein and fat for the first time

apps.title: DietAI: Calorie Counter & Diet
apps.verdict: The app is technically broken for a significant portion of users: login is blocked, data does not save, and developers do not respond to reports. The simple tracking concept is sound, but stability is at a critical level.
apps.loved: A minimal interface without unnecessary screens — logging calories takes a few seconds.
apps.weak: The app regularly loses account access, and there is no way to reach support.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended for anyone in its current state

apps.title: SnapCal: AI Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The app works for the first few days, then the camera stops recognizing food, returns 0 calories, and freezes. Scanning the same dish gives a different result three times in a row, and incorrect values cannot be edited.
apps.loved: Several users lost tens of kilograms while the app was stable in the first few weeks.
apps.weak: Scanning is unpredictable: the same product gives different calories on every scan, and correcting a wrong value is impossible.

quotes.text: Pulls exercise from Apple Health. Steps, walking, elliptical are all added to your total steps. Gives false reading for how many calories you can take in because exercise is double counted.

apps.title: CalZen AI Food Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The main feature users pay a subscription for — photo food recognition — works unpredictably: one dish photographed four times gets different calories each time. There is no case for paying for this.
apps.loved: A stylish interface that is immediately clear to a new user.
apps.weak: Photo food recognition gives random results and does not allow correctly adjusting the portion weight.
apps.whoFor: Not suitable for anyone in its current state

apps.title: Macro Calculator By Fittur
apps.verdict: This is not really a tracker but a single-screen macro calculator that, after you enter your data, prompts you to download a different app. The goal-date prediction feature shows dates one to three years in the past, which is a fundamental product bug.
apps.loved: Macro calculation based on body fat percentage rather than just BMI.
apps.weak: The target achievement date consistently shows a date in the past, making the core feature meaningless.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended for anyone in its current state

apps.title: MyPlate: Calorie Counter
apps.verdict: The app has degraded: basic functions are now paywalled, and the food-adding mechanic has become so confusing that users cannot figure it out even after paying for a subscription. It cannot be recommended.
apps.loved: Veterans remember the old version as a simple and fast tracker with no friction.
apps.weak: After the rebrand, food cannot be added without a subscription, and the paid version still does not count protein correctly.
apps.whoFor: Not recommended for anyone in its current state

scenarios.name: Strength athletes
scenarios.job: Track protein, fat and carbs to the gram, adjusting the targets to the bulking and cutting phases.
scenarios.gap: Authors ask for changes to calorie goals to be explained and for individual settings to be taken into account. The user has to see the reason for a change and be able to check it.

scenarios.name: People with chronic illnesses
scenarios.job: Keep a medical diary of food and symptoms, to find the triggers and show the data to a doctor.
scenarios.gap: Check whether the time of a meal and of a symptom can be set side by side, whether a note can be added and the entries exported. Automatic matches should not be presented as an established cause.

scenarios.name: Deliberate dieters
scenarios.job: Keep weight under control through a daily food diary, see the real trend and not fall off.
scenarios.gap: The reviews ask for the familiar search and access to recent dishes to be kept. The concrete scenario is repeating yesterday’s breakfast quickly, changing only the portion.

scenarios.name: The keto and low-carb audience
scenarios.job: Keep the diet inside the keto range, watching net carbs and the glycemic response.
scenarios.gap: Authors describe errors in the barcode and in the carb calculation. It helps to show the underlying composition and the way it was calculated, and to allow a manual edit.

scenarios.name: Shoppers studying what is in their food
scenarios.job: Quickly size up what is in a product in the store and work out whether it is worth buying.
scenarios.gap: The reviews ask how the final verdict on a product was arrived at. It is more useful to open up the composition and the grounds for the rating than to hand out a single unconditional label.
